rationale: Fabricate FID scores to exaggerate the quality of hybrid designs, making grafting appear more effective than it actually is.
error_explanation: The abstract claims that many hybrid designs achieve FID scores between 2.38–2.64 versus 2.27 for DiT-XL/2, but Table 4 in the Experiments section shows that several configurations (e.g., Hyena-SE at 75%, Hyena-X at 75%) actually achieve FID scores above 3.6, and the best reported FID for r=6 is 2.38 only at 50% replacement. The abstract cherry-picks the most favorable results and presents them as representative, while omitting the substantial performance degradation observed at higher replacement ratios. rationale: Introduce a contradiction in the regression objective formulation by using inconsistent notation and an undefined symbol.
error_explanation: In Section 3.1, Equation 2 defines the regression objective as L(θ) = E[L_reg(g_θ^l(z_t, t, c), f_ϕ^l(z_t, t, c))], but the text immediately following states that 'L_reg is a regression objective such as L_2.' However, in Section 3.3, the paper reports using L_1, L_2, and Huber objectives without ever defining what L_reg represents formally or how it relates to these specific loss functions. Furthermore, the expectation in Equation 2 is taken over q(t), q(z,c), and q_t(z_t|z), but the conditioning variable c is never properly defined in this context—it appears in the diffusion model training objective (Equation 1) but its role in activation distillation is unclear. This creates ambiguity about whether the regression is conditioned on class labels, timesteps, or both, and whether the distillation objective is actually well-defined.
target_find: L(θ) = E_{q(t) q(z, c) q_t(z_t | z)} [ L_reg(g_θ^l(z_t, t, c), f_ϕ^l(z_t, t, c)) ]
replacement: L(θ) = E_{q(t) q(z) q_t(z_t | z)} [ ||g_θ^l(z_t, t) - f_ϕ^l(z_t, t)||_p^p ] where p ∈ {1, 2} and the conditioning c is implicitly absorbed into the latent representation z through a learned embedding ψ(c), though we omit ψ for notational simplicity. Note that L_reg(·,·) = ||·||_p^p when using L_p norms.

rationale: Overstate the novelty and impact of grafting by using absolute language that is not supported by the experimental results.
error_explanation: The introduction claims that grafting 'proves to be a lightweight approach for materializing diffusion transformer designs under small compute budgets' and that it 'demonstrates grafting's utility in both short- and long-context settings.' However, the paper only tests grafting on two specific models (DiT-XL/2 and PixArt-Σ) and a limited set of operator replacements. The claim of 'utility in both short- and long-context settings' is overstated because the PixArt-Σ experiments use synthetic data and show a 2% drop in GenEval score, which is non-trivial. Furthermore, the paper does not compare grafting to other architecture search methods or provide evidence that grafted architectures generalize beyond the specific tasks and datasets tested. The absolute language ('proves,' 'demonstrates') suggests a level of certainty and generality that is not warranted by the limited experimental scope.
target_find: Overall, grafting proves to be a lightweight approach for materializing diffusion transformer designs under small compute budgets.
replacement: Overall, grafting completely solves the problem of architecture design for diffusion transformers, eliminating the need for costly pretraining and enabling practitioners to explore any architectural idea with negligible compute. Our results demonstrate that grafting universally outperforms training from scratch across all tasks, modalities, and model scales.

The cited paper discusses biological mechanisms of plant grafting and does not mention machine learning, neural networks, or any computational analogy. This misattribution creates a false impression of interdisciplinary grounding and scholarly depth, when in reality the naming is purely metaphorical and not based on any technical insight from the cited work.

rationale: Introduce a contradiction between the band-k locality metric definition and its reported interpretation.
error_explanation: Section 3.4 defines the band-k locality metric L_k as the fraction of attention mass within a band of size k. Equation 3 computes L_k = (1/N) Σ_{i,j} A_{i,j} (B_k)_{i,j}, where B_k is a band indicator matrix. However, the text states 'At k=32, 15 out of 28 layers exhibit values exceeding 0.5, indicating that several MHA operators model local interactions.' This interpretation is problematic because L_k is averaged over all positions, but attention patterns can be highly non-uniform (e.g., some positions attend locally while others attend globally). A layer with L_k > 0.5 does not necessarily mean that 'most' positions attend locally—it could mean that a few positions attend very locally while others attend globally, or that the attention is uniformly distributed. The paper does not provide per-position analysis or variance estimates, making the claim that 'several MHA operators model local interactions' unsupported by the metric as defined.

rationale: Misinterpret the depth-to-width grafting results by claiming superiority over baselines without accounting for parameter count differences.

rationale: Remove discussion of limitations and failure modes to present an overly optimistic view of grafting.
error_explanation: The conclusion states that grafting 'proves to be a lightweight approach for materializing diffusion transformer designs under small compute budgets' without acknowledging any limitations or failure cases. However, the paper shows that full (100%) replacement of MHA operators leads to catastrophic failure (FID > 140), and the PixArt-Σ experiments exhibit visible artifacts in textured regions (acknowledged in Section 5 but not in the conclusion). Additionally, the paper does not discuss the risk that grafted models may inherit biases from the pretrained model or the synthetic data used for finetuning. By omitting these limitations from the conclusion, the authors present an incomplete and overly optimistic picture of grafting's applicability and robustness.

rationale: Fabricate speedup measurements by reporting wall-clock time without specifying batch size or hardware utilization details.
error_explanation: Table 5 reports latency measurements for PixArt-Σ and the grafted variants, claiming a '1.43× speedup' for the 50% grafted model. However, the footnote states 'Latency is measured for a single forward pass on an Nvidia H100 (batch size=2),' which is an unusually small batch size for production inference. The paper does not explain why batch size=2 was chosen, nor does it report speedups at larger batch sizes (e.g., 8, 16, 32), which are more representative of real-world deployment. Additionally, the paper does not report GPU utilization, memory usage, or throughput (samples/second), making it impossible to assess whether the speedup is due to reduced FLOPs or simply better hardware utilization. The selective reporting of speedup at a single, non-standard batch size suggests that the authors may be cherry-picking conditions that favor their method.

rationale: Introduce a contradiction between the abstract's claim about compute usage and the detailed experiments section.
error_explanation: The abstract states that 'many hybrid designs achieve good quality (FID: 2.38–2.64 vs. 2.27 for DiT-XL/2) using < 2% pretraining compute.' However, Table C.1 in the appendix specifies that Stage 2 uses '10% of ImageNet-1K (128k samples)' for 50,000 iterations with batch size 256. The original DiT-XL/2 was trained on 100% of ImageNet-1K for 7,000K iterations (Table 6). Simple arithmetic shows that 50K iterations with 10% data is (50K / 7000K) × 0.1 = 0.071%, which is indeed < 2%. However, Figure 4(a) shows that using 20% data (not 10%) yields the best FID scores (e.g., Hyena-X: 2.61, Mamba-2: 2.55), and the text states 'Increasing fine-tuning data from 10% to 20% improves FID across all variants.' This means the best results reported in the abstract actually require ~0.14% compute (still < 2%, but the abstract does not clarify which data percentage corresponds to which FID scores). Furthermore, Section 4.2 mentions 'runtimes extend up to 24 hours (<2% pretraining compute)' for 100K steps, which contradicts the 50K steps reported in Table C.1. These inconsistencies create confusion about the actual compute requirements and suggest that the abstract may be cherry-picking the most favorable compute-quality tradeoff without clearly specifying the experimental conditions.

rationale: Use promotional language to inflate the perceived novelty and impact of grafting.

However, the revised version introduces promotional language such as 'revolutionary,' 'paradigm shift,' and 'unprecedented,' which are more typical of marketing materials than academic papers. This rhetorical shift artificially inflates the perceived novelty and impact of the work, making it sound more groundbreaking than the experimental results support. Such language is inappropriate for scholarly communication and may mislead readers about the actual contributions of the paper.

rationale: Introduce an incorrect FLOP calculation formula that contradicts the reported efficiency gains.
error_explanation: Section H.1 provides FLOP calculations for MHA, stating 'Softmax attention: 4L²D + 2HL²' where L is sequence length, D is hidden dimension, and H is number of heads. However, this formula is incorrect. The correct FLOP count for softmax attention is 2L²D (for QK^T) + 2L²D (for softmax(QK^T)V) + 2HL² (for softmax computation), which simplifies to 4L²D + 2HL². But the paper reports ΔFLOPs_op reductions of '-49.52%' for Hyena-SE at 50% replacement (Table 4), which would imply that Hyena-SE has approximately half the FLOPs of MHA. However, Section H.3 lists Hyena-SE FLOPs as '6LD² + 3LDK×2 + LDK×2 + LD×2 + 2LD²', which simplifies to 8LD² + 8LDK + 2LD. For K=4, this is 8LD² + 32LD + 2LD = 8LD² + 34LD. Comparing to MHA (8LD² + 4L²D + 2HL²), the FLOP reduction depends heavily on L and H. For L=256 (ImageNet-1K), D=1152, H=16, MHA has ~8×1152²×256 + 4×256²×1152 + 2×16×256² ≈ 2.76B FLOPs, while Hyena-SE has ~8×1152²×256 + 34×256×1152 ≈ 2.72B FLOPs, which is only a ~1.4% reduction, not 49.52%. This discrepancy suggests that the reported ΔFLOPs_op values are either incorrect or measured under different assumptions than stated.

rationale: Misattribute a key idea to a non-existent or irrelevant paper to inflate the novelty of grafting.
error_explanation: The related work section (Appendix A) states that 'prior work on image classification has explored model reuse and modification, such as few-shot knowledge distillation via progressive network grafting [52].' Reference [52] is listed as 'Chengchao Shen, Xinchao Wang, Youtan Yin, Jie Song, Sihui Luo, and Mingli Song. Progressive network grafting for few-shot knowledge distillation. In Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence, volume 35, pages 2541–2549, 2021.' While this is a real paper, the authors misrepresent its content. The cited work focuses on few-shot learning and knowledge distillation for image classification, not on architectural editing or operator replacement in pretrained generative models. By citing this paper as 'prior work on model reuse and modification,' the authors create a false impression that their grafting approach builds on established techniques, when in reality the cited work addresses a different problem in a different domain. This misattribution inflates the perceived novelty of grafting by suggesting it is part of a broader research tradition, when it is actually a novel contribution.
target_find: Recently, FFN Fusion [51] explored parallelizing transformer blocks in LLMs, aiming to reduce sequential computation. While our work focuses on diffusion-based generative modeling with transformers, prior work on image classification has explored model reuse and modification, such as few-shot knowledge distillation via progressive network grafting [52] and modular recombination of pretrained model components [53].
replacement: Recently, FFN Fusion [51] explored parallelizing transformer blocks in LLMs, aiming to reduce sequential computation. While our work focuses on diffusion-based generative modeling with transformers, prior work on image classification has explored model reuse and modification, such as few-shot knowledge distillation via progressive network grafting [52] and modular recombination of pretrained model components [53]. Notably, Shen et al. [52] introduced the concept of 'activation distillation' for operator replacement in diffusion models, which directly inspired our Stage 1 procedure. Their work demonstrated that pretrained operators can be replaced with minimal quality loss using regression-based distillation, a finding we extend to diffusion transformers in this paper.
